item.title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
item.description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Bank of America stock falls in the wake of a historic $1.2 billion fine after it failed to report financial crime
item.description:
Bank of America has been fined over $1.2 billion for violating anti-money-laundering and sanction laws. 

On Tuesday, October 13, the U.S. Department of the Treasury handed down the fine, stating that Bank of America had failed to report over $5 billion in “suspicious activity” to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). 

Over $1 billion of the activity was “national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury stated in its announcement. 

“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risk,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Third largest in history

The $1.2 billion fine is the Treasury Department’s third largest in its history. In 2023, it fined Binance $3.4 billion and, a year later, fined TD Bank $1.3 billion. 

The total figure includes a $750 million fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)—the largest in its history—for having an “ineffective” anti-money laundering program. 

It also comprised an $11.6 million settlement agreement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). While this is the smallest part of the fine, the 475 “apparent violations of sanction programs” are quite notable. These sanctions were against Russia, Iran, global terrorism, and narcotics, among other significant areas. 

According to the Treasury, “these apparent violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error.”

“We are responsible for getting it right”

Reached for comment by Fast Company, a Bank of America spokesperson said the financial services giant has invested “billions of dollars” in financial crime and is committed to addressing the issues raised by U.S. regulators.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 OCC Consent Order and FinCEN’s investigation.”

Stock down after third-quarter earnings

Shares of Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC) were down more than 8% on Wednesday following the fine and an early-morning earnings report.

The company reported $30.12 billion in revenue for quarter three, falling short of Wall Street’s predicted $30.69 billion, according to consensus estimates cited by CNBC.

“Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share,” Bank of America’s statement said. “We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base.”

item.title: Why Does Saudi Arabia Struggle to Stop Houthi Attacks?
The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Washington Cannot Outsource Saudi Security to the Mecca Pact
item.description:
The Houthis have significantly escalated their airstrike campaign targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, with two consecutive attacks at Riyadh’s international airport, killing 12 and injuring 300 others between October 10 and 11. The Houthis’ deadly strike campaign has exposed an uncomfortable truth that Saudi Arabia’s newest defense alliance cannot yet guarantee its security. Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani leaders activated the Mecca Pact on October 5, but the Riyadh airport attacks demonstrated how little a collective-defense declaration means to an adversary willing to keep firing. Riyadh needs more than diplomatic solidarity and bare-minimum defense support, which are not willing to undertake kinetic engagements with the Houthis. Washington should expand military assistance to Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognized government without rushing into another open-ended bombing campaign. The United States has greater strategic interests at stake than either Ankara or Islamabad, and capabilities the new pact cannot quickly replicate.

Saudi Energy Security Is American Security

Saudi Arabia remains a central American security partner and an indispensable player in global energy markets. With Iranian attacks and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, the kingdom’s East-West Pipeline has become a critical alternative for moving crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline throughput reportedly reached approximately 5.8 million barrels per day in early October, while roughly four million barrels per day have been rerouted around Hormuz.

This arrangement, however, remains vulnerable to external attacks that can disrupt the flow of energy from the Middle East. Drone attacks forced a temporary pipeline shutdown in late September, although Saudi Arabia attributed those strikes to Iran-backed Iraqi militias. The Houthis have separately attacked and threatened Saudi energy facilities. And despite a September rebound to 16.3 million barrels per day, Middle Eastern crude exports remained below their prewar level of 19.5 million. A prolonged Saudi-Houthi war could jeopardize the infrastructure and confidence sustaining that fragile recovery.

Security threats to Saudi Arabia also complicate ongoing and future diplomatic gains with Riyadh, especially considering President Donald Trump’s vision to have Saudi Arabia join the Abraham Accords. The US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation agreement, signed in July and submitted for congressional review in August, promises a long-term economic and strategic relationship. While its proliferation safeguards deserve rigorous scrutiny, escalating security threats could complicate implementation and diminish Washington’s influence over Saudi nuclear choices. Pakistan and Turkey have interests in Saudi stability; the United States has energy, maritime, defense-industrial, and nonproliferation interests simultaneously.

Pakistan Has Too Many Fronts of Its Own

The pact’s most acute capacity problem lies in Pakistan. Islamabad must contain the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Baloch separatist violence while guarding a contested frontier with Afghanistan and maintaining forces opposite India. These are not hypothetical distractions but serious battlefield challenges for Islamabad, which is fighting on multiple fronts simultaneously. Pakistan conducted airstrikes inside Afghanistan on October 1, amid recurring border clashes. On October 11, Islamabad imposed emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, citing worsening militancy, although the opposition disputes the justification. Additionally, the India frontier remains an enduring contingency that Pakistani planners cannot discount. This threat landscape will create serious bandwidth issues for Pakistan’s military in the immediate to near term, further limiting Islamabad’s support for Riyadh.

Pakistan’s armed forces can provide specialized assistance abroad, but sustained expeditionary commitments require personnel, logistics, and strategic attention. Pakistani officials have dismissed Western media reports of its troop presence in government-controlled territories of Yemen. Still, the death of a Pakistani driver in a Houthi drone strike in Marib, Yemen, has brought Pakistan’s actual role within the defense pact under scrutiny—whether Islamabad is taking up a direct combat role alongside the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces on the ground. On the other hand, Turkey has formidable drones, electronic-warfare expertise, and NATO experience, but its priorities extend from Syria and Iraq to the Eastern Mediterranean. Neither country should be dismissed as a partner, and neither should be treated as an unlimited strategic reserve for a war with no clear end date.

Bab al-Mandeb Is Washington’s Problem Too

The constant threat of disrupting commercial vessel traffic in the Red Sea makes American restraint increasingly difficult. Washington and the Houthis have recently reached an understanding that the group will not target non-Saudi ships in the Red Sea given that the United States does not undertake kinetic strikes targeting Houthi infrastructure in Yemen. This is a non-binding understanding and dangerously shortsighted, which offers no permanent guarantee that the Houthis would never threaten Bab al-Mandeb again. If the Houthis begin losing territory rapidly to the government forces, they are highly likely to use every means possible to threaten commercial vessels in the Red Sea. This is right out of their counterpart Iran’s coercion playbook around Hormuz, illustrating the leverage a regional actor can extract from a chokepoint without maintaining a total blockade.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have made meaningful gains along the western coast of Yemen over the past week. The anti-Houthi coalition of Yemeni forces reportedly retook Perim Island and al Aradi after securing Jabal Kahbub, an operationally significant hilltop which overlooks the frontlines between the Houthi rebels and government forces. Saudi Close Air Support helped enable the counteroffensive, which was partially successful because Houthi positions elsewhere on the Red Sea coast still pose threats against commercial shipping. Bottom line is that the loss of terrain nearest the strait does not eliminate the maritime risk.

Conclusion

Limited tactical success to the credit of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces should not be conflated with larger operational achievements against the Houthis. Washington should therefore expand real-time targeting support, aerial refueling, integrated air and missile defense, counter-drone capabilities, and maritime surveillance. It should help Saudi and Yemeni forces protect infrastructure and hold recovered ground, while keeping the threshold for direct US strikes explicit: demonstrable threats to American forces, international navigation, or sustained attacks that overwhelm partner defenses. Any strikes must be narrowly targeted, legally justified, and paired with a diplomatic off-ramp.

There is precedent, but also a warning. During Operation Rough Rider, US forces struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets between March and May 2025. The campaign ended in May without destroying the movement but severely degraded the group’s missile production infrastructure. Washington knows how to hit Houthi infrastructure, a task which Turkey and Pakistan are hesitant to and most likely incapable of undertaking. Bipartisan backing for Saudi defense would strengthen this approach, but it cannot compensate for strategic passivity. The Mecca partners can share the burden, but they cannot yet carry it alone. America should neither outsource Saudi security to an untested pact nor inherit Yemen’s entire war. Washington must provide the military support necessary to safeguard its strategic interests while making clear that further Houthi escalation will invite a more forceful, direct US military response.

item.title: The Next War of Attrition is in Yemen
item.description:
Battlefield dynamics in Yemen shift quickly, but Houthi aims do not. A movement organized around radical ideology and perpetual conflict now shares a border with a state organized around modernization and prosperity. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis both have formidable but very different military capabilities, and neither can force a quick decision on the other. That is the recipe for a long war of attrition. The closest precedent is the war in Ukraine, to which the Yemen war is increasingly linked, and which may be instructive for the Kingdom on how best to prepare.

There is also a parallel to be made with the related conflict between Iran and the United States, the fallout from which has severely affected the GCC countries, including Saudi Arabia. Essentially, we are witnessing the leverage of a lesser military force when that party has a much higher threshold for pain and disruption than the stronger party. Iran and the Houthis are both betting that the Saudis are sufficiently anxious to hold on to their peaceful model of business, tourism, energy and investment to settle at almost any price and end the present conflict.

The Houthi mindset

The Houthi ideological program is anti-Saudi, anti-American, anti-Israel, anti-democratic, anti-liberal and antisemitic. It has long cast the Saudi monarchy as an American-Israeli puppet unworthy of the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. Some of this is personal: The father of Abdelmalek al-Houthi, the group's leader, clashed for years with Saudi-backed clerics and was rumored to have been targeted for assassination at their behest.

But the grievances against the Kingdom also has a territorial dimension. In the 1934 Treaty of Taif,

Imam Yahya of northern Yemen settled the border with the Saudi state and ceded Jizan, Asir, and Najran provinces. The Houthis, who present themselves somewhat ambiguously as heirs to the imamate, have revived claims to all three provinces. The purpose is to stoke resentment of the Saudis and to leave the Kingdom's southern border unsettled. This territorial dimension intersects with the allegation that the Saudis are not fit to control Mecca and Medina: Abdelmalik recently reiterated that Mecca belongs to the Islamic Umma, rather than being a province of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis implicitly – and sometimes explicitly – claim the whole of the southern half of the Arabian Peninsula, “from Mecca to Mahra”.

The deeper reason the Houthis cannot stop is structural. The Houthis depend on mobilization, and for a movement of that kind peace is a threat rather than a reward. Conflict is what holds the project together, as it justifies extracting resources from an impoverished population, excuses unpaid salaries and collapsed services, and lets the security apparatus treat every critic as a collaborator. For a deeply unpopular regime, war with Saudi Arabia and its local Yemeni partners is the most useful conflict available and could yield significant returns if the Houthis can extract concessions at the negotiating table. It was already clear during Ambassador Fitton-Brown’s period of responsibility for Yemen that the perverse incentives of the war economy meant that Houthi negotiator Muhammad Abdelsalam was viewed with suspicion by Houthi field commanders, who were benefitting from the war economy and associated “respect”, and had no interest in being transformed into administrators with responsibility to balance their power.

The Houthi menu

The Houthis approach is predatory: isolate each victim and deal with it alone. They pursue bilateral deals that peel off potential adversaries, and calibrate each attack so the victim would conclude that a limited response is cheaper than a sustained one. They have cultivated the sense that they are somebody else's problem, Israel's when they fire missiles at Eilat, Riyadh's when they strike Abha, etc. A decade on, the Houthis have have attacked many different states, and yet no one has owned the problem.

It is troubling that US negotiators have recently sat with the Houthis in Muscat and apparently taken at face value Houthi assurances that their quarrel is only with the Saudis, not with American – or even the Israelis! All this while threatening the US economy and risking the lives of US nationals at civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom.

In the current round of fighting, the Houthis have three key options for escalation.

The first is domestic expansion within Yemen. It is the least risky for the regime because it stays within a conflict the world has learned to ignore. New territory brings new populations to tax, new ports and crossings to control, and new momentum to display at home. The drawback is that this also pushes the Zaidi Houthis deeper and deeper into Shafa’I (Sunni) territory, where the population is hostile to their agenda.

The second option is maritime. Attacks on commercial vessels and Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab inflict harm, especially in the economic realm, and they are extremely difficult to deter and defend against. The drawback is that shipping is a global interest, albeit somewhat elastic, and so a sustained campaign against it may invite the involvement of states with maritime commercial interests that would otherwise stay out of a Saudi-Houthi war. It also, by violating the Law of the Sea, provides an unimpeachable legal basis to build an international military coalition against them.

The third option, targeting civilian aviation, is the riskiest. A recent Houthi attack, on October 10, killed at least twelve people in the deadliest attack on the Kingdom in more than a decade. One US national was among the dead. The strikes came with a threat to airlines, "for the last time," to stay out of Saudi airspace. This type of attack is probably the most likely to galvanize an international coalition and demonstrates that the Houthis have an extremely high appetite for risk.

The Houthis are testing how far they can take this. Downing a passenger aircraft would almost certainly bring the overwhelming response, including direct American strikes, that the Houthis have spent recent decades seeking to avoid (albeit with an imperfect record). The threat alone can inflict some damage to Saudi Arabia, so the threats will continue. Whether the Houthis will continue or even take escalation in this realm even further will depend on whether they believe anyone would make them pay.

The wars are already connected

It might be tempting to treat the Russia-Ukraine and Houthi-Saudi comparison as merely illustrative, but the two wars are materially linked in both directions.

Russia’s involvement with the Houthis is the most direct link thus far. By mid-2024, Russia had recruited hundreds, possibly even thousands, of Yemeni men for the Ukrainian front through a Houthi-linked network operating out of Oman. Also, during the Houthi Red Sea campaign of 2023 to 2025, Russia reportedly passed satellite targeting data to the Houthis. And the Shahed-136 that Iran supplied to Russia, which Russia now mass-produces and improved upon, belongs to the same family of weapon the Houthis fire at Saudi infrastructure. Russian innovation may yet flow back through Tehran to Sanaa.

Russia’s public posture toward the Houthi problem has been one of ostensible concern. In September, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov called Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian targets “unacceptable,” and President Putin and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman discussed freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab by phone. Riyadh should not mistake this for neutrality: Moscow treats the Houthis as a pawn in a larger game.

The mechanism is not complicated. A crisis on the Arabian Peninsula drains Western attention and, perhaps more importantly, Western munitions. In late March, the Pentagon was reported to be weighing whether to divert air defense interceptors bought for Ukraine to the Middle East, because the war with Iran was straining stocks of critical American munitions. This is the outcome Moscow has been working toward since it abstained on the 2015 arms embargo against the Houthis and then spent a decade obstructing the UN panel that documented its violations. Russia does not need the Houthis to win; it needs them to keep fighting. It makes a similar calculation over supporting continuing Iranian resistance to the Americans.

The link is starting to run the other way too. Kyiv’s growing ties with Saudi Arabia are more recent but no less consequential. On March 27, the two countries signed a defense cooperation agreement centered on counter-drone expertise. More than two hundred Ukrainian anti-drone specialists are now deployed in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, and Riyadh is reportedly negotiating a large purchase of Ukrainian interceptor drones that cost between one and three thousand dollars each. Until recently Riyadh was deepening ties with Moscow through OPEC+ and BRICS, and yet it is now importing Ukrainian expertise to defend against weapons Moscow helped perfect.

Saudi Arabia's dilemma

As in Eastern Europe, no quick decision is likely in the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The Houthis cannot be bombed out of Sanaa, as the coalition learned between 2015 and 2022. While the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive along the coast has stabilized the front and claimed gains around Mokha, it remains a long way from the capital. That leaves Riyadh with three paths, none of them are likely to be easy.

The first is appeasement, which would feed the movement. Since June, the Houthis have demanded a deal that lifts the blockade on their ports and airports and restores the flow of cash into Sanaa. Such a deal would ease the regime’s revenue crisis and pay for its next tranche of weapons. The Kingdom tried a version of this approach after 2022, and the result is the war it is fighting now.

The second is deterrence, which fails against an adversary that seeks out perpetual conflict. Deterrence assumes an enemy that weighs costs and benefits in measurements that the Saudis understand, and that appears not to be the case. For a movement like the Houthis whose legitimacy rests on “resistance,” conflict is not only a hazard but also a realization of an extremist aspiration.

The third is defeating the Houthis outright, which means returning to a war Saudi Arabia already fought and abandoned. A strategy that could succeed does exist: cut Houthi supply lines of cash and other material while backing a unified Yemeni ground campaign under a single command. But this will require sustained pressure over time in order to crack the Houthi defenses and then ultimately the regime.

Attrition, then, is the most reasonable path forward. The question is not whether Saudi Arabia will be in a long war but whether it will be prepared for one. Attrition is survivable for the side that innovates and devastating for the side that assumes the war will end in a quick and decisive maneuver. The length of the war also introduces uncertainties about changes in the posture of allies, especially the US. There is a need to bake in bipartisan agreement in Washington, DC, that it is a US national security interest to ensure that the Saudis, and the Internationally Recognized Government of Yemen, and the Law of the Sea prevail in this conflict.

Two Ukrainian lessons

Ukraine survived attrition against a far larger adversary for two reasons, and both apply to Riyadh.

The first is adaptation. It built a drone industry from almost nothing into one producing millions of systems a year, fielded interceptor drones costing a small fraction of a Patriot missile, and compressed production and procurement timelines.

The Saudi-Ukranian March agreement imports some of that expertise but may not necessarily transfer all of the knowledge necessary to built its own industry. A defense that depends on imports from a country at war is precarious at the best of times.

Riyadh has the money and the stated intent, and Vision 2030 set a goal of localizing half of military spending by the end of the decade. But localization so far has meant licensed assembly of foreign designs rather than innovation under fire. The Kingdom has not reached a wartime tempo in which a new counter-drone system is conceived, tested against live Houthi attacks, and fielded within weeks. That is the capability Ukraine built and Saudi Arabia lacks.

The second lesson is diplomatic. Ukraine did not survive alone. It built a coalition of dozens of states that supplied weapons, trained its forces, financed its budget, and shared intelligence. For the Houthis, a coalition of this kind is the worst possible development, and it is exactly what their strategy of isolating victims and claiming false symmetry is meant to prevent.

The current war gives Riyadh the chance to build one, but the pieces remain fragmented. Ukraine's example is that a coalition does not assemble itself. It must be rallied, placed under a single command, and given a shared objective beyond absorbing attacks. The Houthis' own escalation, which has now killed citizens of a dozen countries at a single airport, is doing part of that work for Riyadh. The Kingdom's task is to turn condemnation into commitment before the moment passes.

So what would this coalition look like? The Saudis already have a maritime group of 14 that opposes Houthi blackmail against them in the Red Sea. But the US, UAE, UK and the other European powers are not part of it. With US leadership and assistance, this needs to be remedied. This is achievable, on the basis of three compelling legal bases: enforcement of the Law of the Sea; the legitimacy of the Yemeni government (and illegitimacy of the Houthis); and the legitimate defense and self-defense of Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election
item.description:
Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election Expert comment LToremark 15 October 2026

US voters are linking economic concerns to the Trump administration’s foreign policy choices. This is bad news for Republicans.

Foreign policy rarely decides US elections. Conventional wisdom is that voters know little, and care less, about international affairs. Instead, they are driven by pocketbook issues, like the price of gas and groceries. As James Carville, an adviser to Bill Clinton, once observed: ‘it’s the economy, stupid’.  But this year, the economy is foreign policy.

There are two important exceptions to the rule that US voters don’t care about foreign policy – and they both apply this year. One, voters care about foreign affairs when an administration’s choices directly affect their daily lives. Two, voters care about what foreign policy choices reveal about a president’s competence as commander-in-chief. 

The upcoming midterms could therefore be a rare foreign policy election – of a kind not seen since 2006 when a backlash to George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq war handed Republicans a ‘thumping’ defeat. 

With voters now feeling the pain of yet another war in the Middle East and Trump’s tariffs, history could repeat itself. The president seems aware of this risk, sending mixed signals about whether the elections will shape his handling of the war in Iran and striking a deal on diesel exports with Russia to ease the pain at the pump for voters.

But perhaps the bigger question is what Trump does after the midterms, the last major electoral check on his presidency. 

War on the ballot

Become a corporate member

Give your organization access to trusted geopolitical analysis, policy insight and expert networks to help leaders anticipate risk, navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions.

War has always been the clearest example of when foreign policy directly affects the daily lives of voters.

But this is not always reflected in polls about the importance of individual issues – and this year is no different. Voters cite economic issues as the key drivers of their vote. In a recent survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, pluralities of voters across the political spectrum cite inflation and the cost of living as most important to their vote (37 per cent overall). By contrast, only 2 per cent single out the war in Iran as the most important issue, possibly due to the relatively low number of US casualties.

But that does not mean it is not having an impact. Voters are linking the pain in their pocketbooks with the foreign policy choices of this administration. According to a recent survey by the Institute for Global Affairs, 81 per cent of Americans say the war in Iran has increased the cost of living. The Chicago Council survey puts the number even higher, at 86 per cent.

And then there are the trade wars. According to the Chicago Council survey, 81 per cent of respondents say tariffs have been bad for the cost of living. It is unsurprising, therefore, that 75 per cent of Americans say tariffs will be important to their midterm vote, according to a survey by the Cato Institute.

Importantly, these findings cannot be written off as partisanship. Across a whole range of issues, support for Trump’s policies lags well behind his overall approval rating – which continues to hover around a historic low of 37 per cent. This suggests voters are not just instinctively opposing anything the president does but that large numbers of Americans, including many who otherwise support him, do not like his policy choices.

Affordability concerns will still dominate these elections. But large numbers of Americans blame the administration’s foreign policy choices for the perilous state of their household finances. And that’s bad news for Republicans.

From a strong leader to a reckless one

The second exception is when prominent foreign policy missteps tarnish the image of the sitting president in ways that cause voters to take note.

For example, how the Biden administration handled the 2021 US withdrawal from Afghanistan severely damaged perceptions of Joe Biden. His approval rating dropped almost overnight and never recovered.

In 2024, Trump was able to turn this into an advantage on the campaign trail by presenting himself as a strong leader who would stand up against America’s adversaries – and with a commitment to peace.

Today, Trump’s reputation is suffering from both his inability to resolve foreign policy challenges he inherited and the abandonment of his pledge to avoid entangling the US in costly conflicts overseas.

In a CNN/SSRS survey, just 29 per cent of US adults said they approved of Trump’s handling of foreign affairs, down from 42 per cent shortly after he returned to office. Only one in four respondents believed he had a clear strategy for handling Tehran, down from 40 per cent in the immediate aftermath of the outbreak of the war. 

These dynamics also appear to be feeding into broader perceptions of Trump’s leadership. In a YouGov survey fielded at the outset of the war, 56 per cent of respondents said the word ‘reckless’ applied ‘a lot’ to Trump – up five points from a year ago – while the proportion who described him as a ‘strong leader’ dropped four percentage points. 

To what degree will foreign policy shape the results – and how will Trump respond?

Related work

What the US midterms could mean for Trump’s power

Republicans were already likely to fare poorly. The midterms are traditionally seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent president, and with Trump’s overall approval ratings at a near-record low, history is not on his side.

Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference.

In some swing states Republican candidates are distancing themselves from the president’s policies. In Michigan, Senate nominee Mike Rogers has said the war ‘needs to end, and end quickly’, to provide relief for American families. In Iowa, meanwhile, Senate nominee Ashley Hinson similarly said that Iowans ‘shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran’. 

Trump’s diesel deal with Russia indicates some sensitivity to the electoral risks of high gas prices. But achieving this by accommodating Vladimir Putin – rather than an embargo on US diesel exports, for example – has only highlighted another foreign policy weakness: Trump’s inability to end the war in Ukraine.

But will an electoral rebuke result in more foreign policy restraint? Perhaps the most important question is not the degree to which foreign policy will shape the results, but how the president will respond. 

And here, history offers a warning. After his 2006 midterm defeat, President Bush did not change course. Instead, he defied the mandate voters had given by escalating an unpopular war in the Middle East.

President Trump recently pledged not to attack Iran before the midterms, having previously expressed a desire to help his party in the elections. Whether he too will try to end the war through a dramatic escalation once the ballots are counted remains to be seen. 

But he would not be the first president to double down on an unpopular policy once unshackled from electoral constraints. The ‘lame duck’ phase of Trump’s presidency may therefore prove even more disruptive on the international stage.

item.title: Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court
item.description:
Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court Expert comment sfarrell.drupa… 15 October 2026

The US decision to extend sanctions has upped the ante in its campaign against the ICC. The Court’s supporters must decide how to respond, perhaps now it is time to put all options on the table.

On 9 October 2026, the US designated the International Criminal Court under Executive Order 14203, extending its existing sanctions package on individual ICC officials to the entity itself as a whole.

The US imposed asset freezes on any property owned by the Court and prohibited all transactions by US individuals or entities involving the ICC.

The US has allowed certain limited exceptions to this general prohibition, to allow for the ongoing detention of some awaiting trial, the payment of pensions, the use of IT software and social media and a 180-day ‘wind down’, allowing certain otherwise prohibited transactions until April 2027.

These sanctions were introduced by the US in what Secretary of State Marco Rubio called an ongoing campaign to ‘dismantle the ICC brick by brick’.

‘For decades, Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members, or political leaders. America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it,’ Rubio said in a statement.

‘We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer,’ he added.

The ICC called the sanctions ‘an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.’

Those countries that have signed up to the ICC – the ‘State Parties’  – now have to decide how to respond, through diplomacy; support or the ‘nuclear option’.

The impact

An asset freeze essentially prevents making any economic resources available directly or indirectly to the ICC.  They must be observed by all US persons and green card holders, wherever they are in the world, all US companies and any person in the US. 

They also apply to any transactions or data routed through the United States. In reality, this can often limit (at best) and prevent (at worst) nearly all financial transactions of a designated person.

As such, if left unchecked, the US sanctions could severely hamper the day-to-day operations of the ICC.  The General Licence operates to provide a wind down period, but at most provides a stay of execution and the potential for diplomatic efforts to reverse or mitigate the impact.

The Court itself noted that whilst it endeavours to continue functioning as normal, international cooperation is imperative as the Court’s fate also rests in ‘the hands of the States that created it’. 

So far, foreign ministers of the UK and others have issued a Joint Statement affirming their unwavering support for the ICC. The EU has also said that it stands ready ‘to take all necessary measures to ensure the Court continues to operate effectively and fulfils its indispensable mandate’. 

Below are recommendations on how the UK government may best respond to the ICC designation in coalition with other State Parties.

Diplomatic Engagement 

State Parties should open the dialogue as necessary to address the US concerns regarding the authority of the ICC. 

The 180-day Maintenance General Licence, marked as a show of good faith, intends to achieve just that. It provides State Parties the chance for diplomatic engagement.  The ICC’s Assembly of States Parties in December will provide an opportunity to review and align the response of the State Parties to the US.

Practical Support: Preparing for the Worst

In parallel to diplomatic efforts, State Parties can start to consider what practical assistance they can provide in the event that diplomatic efforts are unsuccessful or that companies start de-risking sooner rather than later and start to withdraw services before the expiry of the US General Licences that could impact – as no doubt the US intends – the ongoing investigations and operations of the Court.

As such, whilst the US General Licence might allow for a 180-day ‘wind down’ of the provision of crucial goods and services, companies caught by US sanctions may simply decide to stop working with the Court at any time.

That means the State Parties need a comprehensive plan to support the Court, covering everything from provision of IT to support on banking and payment routes, and everything in between.

Blocking Statute: the Nuclear Option

Some State Parties – in particular the UK and EU Member States – may have the option of turning to the ‘Blocking Statute’.

This has been dubbed the ‘nuclear option’ by Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen. It would essentially prohibit any natural or legal person from complying with US sanctions.

But Blocking Statutes have only been deployed vary rarely in the past, primarily targeting US extra-territorial over-reach where it has imposed sanctions against countries like Cuba and Iran, and required those outside of US jurisdiction to comply with them.

However, even this nuclear option’ is not without its limitations. First, it won’t be available to all State Parties without new primary legislation. Second, even where the legislation is in place, it is not clear that the US measures would fall squarely within the legislation which is designed to protect ‘trading interests’ against extra-territorial measures. An argument could certainly be made, but it could face challenge if ever relied upon.

Third, it only applies to those caught by the relevant jurisdiction. In the UK and EU, for example, the prohibition on complying with the US sanctions would only have to be observed by UK/EU nationals, UK/EU companies or those operating in the UK or EU.

Finally, it essentially puts domestic companies between a rock and a hard place – fail to comply with US sanctions or fail to comply with the UK/EU ‘Blocking Statute’.

State Parties with this potential option have not deployed it despite the US targeting of judges and Court staff; perhaps now the US has upped the ante in its campaign against the Court, it is time for its supporters to put all options on the table.

What Beijing Calls Open, Washington Should Call an Operation
item.description:
China is about to run the largest influence operation in history. It will not have to run it. The world will download it.

EXPERT PERSPECTIVE -- Our research team at Vanderbilt spent months inside the internal documents of GoLaxy, a Beijing firm - with ties to the Chinese state - that built a machine for shaping opinion abroad. Using AI, it generates personas, amplifies narratives that are favorable to Beijing and buries narratives that are not. And it’s been busy. It was used in Hong Kong to combat dissent against the National Security Law. It was used in Taiwan to sway the island’s 2024 [HWR1] elections.

Now consider what happens when it does not need to be built at all. If Chinese open-weight models — the ones that anyone can download, modify and run on their own machines — become the foundation that the world builds on, then the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) framing of Taiwan, Tiananmen, Xinjiang and Beijing itself ships inside every product that sits on top. No personas. No campaign. Just the default answer, everywhere. Something like this would make GoLaxy look like a dress rehearsal.

And here is the part that should stop Washington cold. Chinese models are about to be everywhere, and American strategy could allow it to happen. Washington is deciding whether to let frontier development run while clamping down on powerful open-weight models (whose safeguards can be stripped away). Here’s the deal though: restrictions would not kill demand for a cheap model that a company can download and make its own. China is standing at the counter with exactly that.

Today, we talk about the AI race as if it has one finish line. But it has two. The first is for frontier capability: who builds the most advanced models. American companies lead the way today. The second finish line is for reach: whose models become the foundation on which thousands of products are built? Chinese firms may have the advantage on this one. The first brings concentrated scientific, economic and military power. The second decides whose systems become the workhorses of ordinary life, and that reach shapes what people know and will learn in the future.

American frontier models like Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are closed, meaning you use them on the company's servers, and the company can cut off access. Chinese developers compete by releasing cheap open-weight models that companies can run on their own, with no provider to answer to. The babysitter has left the building.

This has already started. Airbnb relies on Alibaba's Qwen in its customer-service agent. Qwen, even briefly, powered a tool for searching proposed regulations on the Federal Register website. Amazon says thousands of customers have deployed DeepSeek through its cloud. In every case the interface is American. But the model underneath it is not.

Here’s something else to consider: Chinese developers must operate under Communist Party rules about what may be said. Those rules then shape which questions the models answer, which facts they omit and how they frame sensitive subjects. Open weights can be retuned, but scrubbing built-in defaults is expensive, and most companies will focus their efforts on addressing what matters to their business rather than check how a model handles every political subject. If a cheap Chinese model sits under thousands of products, its habits travel with it — into research tools, classroom software and fact-checkers — and the person on the other end never knows.

Beijing already knows about this risk. When Meta released its open-weight Llama models, Chinese regulators worried that a foreign model could "poison" China's AI ecosystem with information that the CCP censors. It seems to make sense that Washington should take seriously a vulnerability that Beijing recognized first.

None of this makes the open-weight safety problem smaller. In fact, just the opposite. Once a powerful open-weight model is released, its developer cannot recall it. Its safeguards can be stripped away and the model can be used for cyberattacks, the creation of biological weapons or worse. If we’re going to address this as a society, then testing requirements, liability rules and release restrictions are needed. But a Chinese open-weight model carries the same dangerous capabilities as an American one, and no American rule touches it.

If we constrain American developers and leave foreign weights untouched, demand will certainly shifts toward Chinese models. Theoretically, Washington could end up regulating the companies it can see while deepening its own dependence on the ones it cannot.

One answer might be to ban the Chinese models. But that means telling Americans which information technology they may use — and here lies the irony: the openness that protects Americans from domestic censorship may leave them exposed to systems built under Chinese censorship.

TikTok offers a glimpse of the stakes. More than 170 million Americans use it, and tens of millions say they get their news there. Washington spent five years fighting over its recommendation algorithm, and the deal that kept it in the United States required a change to that algorithm. But an algorithm only ranks videos that people make. While that fight dragged on, AI models learned to make the videos themselves — realistic footage with synced audio, from a sentence, in seconds. Three months after the deal closed, TikTok upgraded its ad tools to ByteDance’s newest video model. No rule required anyone to ask whose model was making the videos.

Now, you can see why the United States is facing a trilemma. It wants to prevent the uncontrolled release of dangerous AI capabilities. It wants to preserve Americans' freedom to choose their technology and information. And it wants to avoid dependence on models that are shaped inside an authoritarian system. It cannot fully secure all three.

Honest regulation starts by admitting that. Before restricting an U.S. model, ask which model developers will pick first. Domestic and foreign models distributed in the United States should face the same tests and the same rules. And companies that build products on a foundation model should have to say whose model it is.

AI leadership combines two things: the capability of a country's best models, and the reach of the models embedded in ordinary life. AI risk also combines two things: what a powerful model might do, and what a ubiquitous one tells people is true. GoLaxy showed us what Beijing can do with a machine to shape a belief. Now, what are we going to do about it?

Mr. Goldstein and Mr. Benson are professors at Vanderbilt University who specialize in national and international security.

item.title: Indian police detain 'cockroach' movement founder Dipke ahead of protest
item.description:
Police detained India’s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups, and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.

The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.

The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away.

“We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke.

“I have not broken any law right now…how can you detain me?” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away.

There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention.

Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest.

Park closed ahead of protest

Authorities closed the central New Delhi park before the protest over the voter-roll revision, which critics say has disenfranchised millions.

Dipke urged supporters to rally at Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, where they had gone to wave the national flag.

Earlier this week, police removed authorisation for Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

On Friday, thousands of security personnel were deployed in parts of the city, with yellow-coloured metal barricades put up at key intersections.

Earlier, Dipke said he was undeterred despite the possibility of being arrested ahead of Friday’s protest.

“Why are you so afraid of cockroaches?” Dipke said.

“I want to tell Narendra Modi that we are not afraid… if waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready,” he said Thursday.

Delhi’s municipal authorities said they were closing the Central Park for two days for “administrative” reasons.

Delhi Police have barred public gatherings around Connaught Place citing concerns about public order and safety.

Violation of the orders would “attract suitable legal action”, police said Thursday, but added that they would allow “selected persons” to gather at a “suitable place”.

In recent days, the Indian capital has seen street protests over a large-scale voter roll revision exercise overseen by chief election commissioner Kumar.

Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

On Friday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh dismissed the allegations, saying the sole agenda of the opposition parties was “to destroy democratic institutions and create unrest in the country”.

“Their fight is not for electoral reform… not for Gyanesh Kumar, not for the bright future of the country’s youth,” he said at a news conference.

“Rather, this is their conspiracy to seize power by creating anarchy in the country.”

item.title: The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
item.description:
The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 08:00
Judges in the Gambia v Myanmar case are preparing a ruling that will have ramifications for Israel and Gaza

In the first week of September 2017, Antonia Mulvey was on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, interviewing women and children who had fled across it days earlier.

“Women waited all day to talk to me and they'd had horrific things happen to them,” she told Middle East Eye. “What struck me when I listened to their stories was that they were asking me for justice.”

Mulvey was one of the first three investigators deployed by a UN fact-finding mission. Her brief was sexual violence and crimes against children.

Nine years later, the case that grew out of those accounts is nearing its end, with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) expected to rule in the coming weeks on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Mulvey, now executive director of Legal Action Worldwide (LAW), which represents Rohingya witnesses in the case, said that if the judges rule against Myanmar, it will be the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

For many Rohingya, the ruling is about more than the past. “We need to fix the root cause,” one refugee told LAW researchers. “The best justice for us is to fix the root cause of the problem.”

Legal experts say they also expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

Michael Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, described the case as a "crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide” which, he said, would have "major repercussions" for the South African case.

Decades of persecution

The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority, have lived for generations in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Northern Rakhine was the only part of the country where they formed a majority.

Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law left the Rohingya off the list of the country's officially recognised ethnic groups, leaving most of them stateless. 

The state and its lawyers refer to the Rohingya as “Bengalis”, a term that casts them as migrants from Bangladesh.

For decades, restrictions on the Rohingya’s movement, marriage rights, education and access to healthcare have been documented. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh in waves of violence in 1978, and again in 1991 and 1992. 

In 2012, clashes in Rakhine displaced about 140,000 people, most of them Rohingya. Many remain confined to camps around the state capital, Sittwe. 

“Rohingya have been persecuted in Myanmar for decades,” said Salma, a Rohingya survivor who attended the ICJ hearings in January, in comments shared by LAW. She asked that only her first name be used.

For many refugees, justice now means one thing above all: citizenship. In a survey conducted by LAW of just under 500 refugees in the Cox's Bazar camps in Bangladesh, 86 percent of participants said citizenship and the right to identify as Rohingya were necessary for justice. 

“We want [the] international community to destroy the 1982 law, and we hope they will do it,” one participant said. “We had Myanmar citizenship, and we were living there for a long time, and our citizenship should be restored. If they provide these two things, we will get everything.”

“They want justice, but they want citizenship,” Mulvey said. “They want to be acknowledged for what happened, and they want that land and property back.”

'Clearance operations'

On 25 August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State, after the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) attacked police posts. 

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the months that followed. About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in the camps of Cox's Bazar.

In 2018, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that there was enough information to infer genocidal intent. It called for senior generals - including then-army chief Min Aung Hlaing, who is now president - to be investigated and prosecuted. 

Mulvey said she drafted the report's sections on sexual violence and crimes against children.

“It was the UN fact-finding mission report that Gambia relied upon in order to initiate proceedings at the ICJ,” she said. 

Abubacarr Tambadou, the Gambia's then justice minister, had spent years as a prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He visited the Cox's Bazar camps in 2018. 

In November 2019, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the Gambia filed its case.

The West African country had no direct link to the violence. It relied on the principle, accepted by the court in 2022, that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In January 2020, the court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts. 

A year later, the military seized power. 

In July 2022, the judges rejected Myanmar's objections to the court's jurisdiction, clearing the way for the hearings that took place in January this year.

'It was very silent'

Over three weeks of hearings, the court heard from three Rohingya witnesses in closed session: two men and a woman. They were identified in court only by their initials, and each came from one of three villages at the centre of The Gambia's case: Min Gyi, Maung Nu and Chut Pyin.

Mulvey, their lawyer, said they spoke about the killing of their family members, the sexual violence they had been subjected to and their flight from Rakhine. Two travelled to the Hague from Cox's Bazar and one from Canada, where they had been resettled.

“It was very silent. You could also hear crying. It was extraordinarily powerful testimony,” Mulvey said. “Of course we have to wait to see what the judgment is, but you could feel the weight of it.”

LAW also brought a victims' delegation of three Rohingya survivors to sit in the courtroom: a man, a woman and a hijra, a term used in South Asia for transgender and intersex people. 

Mulvey said it was the first time a transgender survivor had been part of a delegation in the court.

“We did not know that legal proceedings existed, and we could fight for our rights,” Salma, who part of the delegation, said. “But this time, we have the tools to defend ourselves and demand accountability and reparation for what happened to us.” 

Rehana, the delegation's hijra member, who also asked to be identified by her first name only, said she hoped a ruling would include the whole community. “If the genocide is recognised, we hope that we will be getting our justice. Justice for our entire community, including hijra,” she said.

LAW also submitted hundreds of pages of written witness evidence, which Mulvey said The Gambia relied on heavily.

Rape and sexual violence were central to The Gambia's case. “They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice,” Mulvey said, of army soldiers. 

She said investigators found “a pattern of biting, to leave an indelible mark on them”. She said rape in front of the community reflected “the intent to destroy the very social fabric of the community”.

The ICJ has accepted before that rape can be an act of genocide, in Bosnia v Serbia and Croatia v Serbia. But in neither case did it find the intent required to classify those acts as genocide.

A ruling against Myanmar on this point would mark “the first time the ICJ has actually found sexual violence itself to constitute genocide in a merits judgment”, Mulvey said.

What is genocide?

In deciding the case, the judges will draw on the Genocide Convention itself, the court’s own earlier rulings, and the case law of the international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda.

Israel’s war on Gaza: What is the meaning of genocide?
Read More »

The Genocide Convention, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, defines genocide as any of five acts “committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such”. 

In Bosnia v Serbia in 2007, the court held that the intent must be to destroy at least a substantial part of the group, and that it must be physical or biological destruction rather than cultural destruction. 

It also ruled that charges of such exceptional gravity against a state must be proved by evidence that is “fully conclusive”.

Intent can be shown by “particular circumstances” or inferred from a pattern of conduct. But in Croatia v Serbia in 2015, the court set a high bar for inference.

To infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct, it said, “it is necessary and sufficient that this is the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the acts in question”.

Furthermore, applying those tests, the court found in the Bosnia v Serbia case in 2007 that genocide had been committed only at Srebrenica, and that Serbia was responsible for failing to prevent and punish it, not for committing it. 

The Gambia's case

Philippe Sands and Paul Reichler, two lawyers representing the Gambia, argued that Myanmar’s military operations in northern Rakhine State targeted a substantial part of the Rohingya population and that the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy the group.

Sands used Myanmar's own figures from its written pleadings to address whether Myanmar had targeted a “substantial” part of the Rohingya.

'They selected, particularly, women and girls of reproductive age. They gang raped them. That was the method of choice'

- Antonia Mulvey, lawyer

He calculated that 815,459 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine's three townships, Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, before the 2017 operations. About 700,000 of them, nearly nine in 10, fled to Bangladesh. The military “targeted tens of thousands of homes, and over 800,000 human beings”, Sands said.

Myanmar had argued that the estimated 10,000 to 25,000 people killed did not amount to a substantial part of the group. Sands said those figures were “likely to be an underestimate”. 

Myanmar “has gone out of its way to destroy the evidence, including the evidence of the burial of large numbers of bodies in mass graves”, he said.

“Genocide is not a numbers game,” Sands said, explaining that “there is no magical number of victims which turns one kind of crime into another kind of crime.”

“The 700,000 who fled to Bangladesh for their lives were no less targeted than their murdered brothers and sisters,” the British lawyer said.

Sands also argued that northern Rakhine mattered because it was the one region where Rohingya were the majority. 

Turning to intent, he said that it was proved both by “particular circumstances” and by a pattern of conduct. He pointed first to the three witnesses' villages.

“There is no world in which the shooting of Witness MS's daughter, as she waded across a river to escape, was not genocidal; or the intentional burning of his wife and four other children inside a house,” Sands told the court. 

“There is no world in which the gang rape of Witness NJ, the murder of her infant child in front of her, was not genocidal.”

Myanmar acted with genocidal intent, Sands said, because “its discriminatory policies, its hate speech, its pre-planning and organisation, its extreme brutality, its sexual violence, its targeting of children, its destruction of evidence, its impunity for the perpetrators, its failure to co-operate with the UN, cannot reasonably be understood in any other way”.

The counter-terrorism defence

Reichler addressed what is known as the “only reasonable inference” test, which in this case would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

Myanmar's answer was counter-terrorism. “They have put all their eggs in the counter-terrorism basket,” Reichler said.

He told the court that Myanmar's lead counsel, Christopher Staker, had conceded that genocide can take place during a counter-terrorism operation. 

Even if Myanmar was responding to Arsa, he argued, “the fact that there was a counter-terrorism operation in progress … is pure context. It is not intent.”

The question, Reichler said, was what the state intended “at the time its authorised agents began firing their weapons deliberately at Rohingya civilians, including women and children”.

Reichler then dealt with the other possible explanation: that Myanmar meant to drive the Rohingya out, not destroy them. That was the conclusion the court reached about Serbia and Croatia in 2015.

Reichler cited the testimony of the Gambia’s military expert, who was asked whether the operations could have been ethnic cleansing, rather than genocide. The expert said they could not, because ethnic cleansing does not involve killing a group’s children. 

He added that a force seeking only to drive a population out would not keep shooting at people as they fled, or station troops on the river to sink their boats as they were about to reach Bangladesh.

Soldiers also laid landmines at border crossings after 25 August 2017. The fact finding mission said this showed the mines were “intended to target fleeing Rohingya civilians and to prevent those who had already left from returning”.

Russia, Georgia and forced displacement

Reichler contrasted Rakhine with Georgia v Russia, a case in which he had acted for Georgia. 

In this case, Russian forces ordered ethnic Georgians to leave South Ossetia. Those who complied were not harmed. Fleeing refugees were not shot at and there was no systematic sexual violence. “On those facts, if proven, this was forced displacement, or ethnic cleansing. It was not genocide,” Reichler said.

The wars in the former Yugoslavia were “essentially about the control of territory,” he argued. The Tatmadaw, Myanmar's military, “were not seeking to enlarge Myanmar's territory”.

He warned that Myanmar might “change its narrative in the second round, after we have finished speaking and there is no opportunity for us to respond further”.

Mulvey said that is what happened. Myanmar “did not argue deportation or forcible transfer until the very end of their oral hearings”, she told MEE.

In Myanmar’s final session on 29 January, counsel Stefan Talmon quoted one of The Gambia’s own witnesses, identified as MN, telling the court: “We knew that the military did this to force us out of the country.” From such accounts, Talmon argued, the court could conclude that “the intention of the military was not to destroy them as a people as such but to force them out of the country”.

“There is thus at least one other inference that can reasonably be drawn from the conduct,” he said.

Srebrenica genocide survivors draw parallels with Gaza 30 years after massacre
Read More »

But even if expulsion had been the aim, Reichler argued that the court's own judgments allowed for a genocide finding if the displacement was carried out “with a view to the destruction of the group, as distinct from its removal from the region”.

Reichler argued that other motives, such as fighting Arsa, would not rule out genocidal intent. He noted that in Bosnia the court found genocide at Srebrenica even though the Bosnian Serb leadership's “essential motive” was to create a larger Serb state.

What mattered was the intent at the moment Myanmar soldiers were “segregating and executing men and boys, raping and gang raping women and girls, killing children and infants – tossing them into fires”. 

He said the destruction continued well into 2018, including in more than 180 villages where Myanmar admits there was no Arsa activity, and was followed by bulldozing, resettlement by ethnic Rakhine and the building of military bases.

Mulvey described the same pattern from her own investigations. 

“They would surround the village. Then often in the early hours of the morning when people were asleep, they would fire mortars into the village. They would then proceed by shooting indiscriminately at civilians,” she told MEE.

She said soldiers continued to shoot at people as they fled towards Bangladesh. “What they did was to ensure that they were killed along the way,” she said.

Myanmar rejected all the allegations. It argued that the operations were a lawful response to attacks by Arsa.

What western nations argued

In November 2023, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK filed a joint submission to the court in support of the Gambia. 

They were among 11 states that intervened in the case. States that intervene in this way do not comment on the facts, only on how the Genocide Convention should be read.

The six states warned that the “only reasonable inference” test should not be applied so strictly that genocide becomes “near-impossible” to prove, since states rarely put an intent to destroy a group in writing. 

They also argued that the number of people killed should not decide whether genocide took place. Rape, sexual violence and the targeting of children serve no military purpose, so such acts can point strongly to an intent to destroy a group, they wrote. 

The six states added that UN fact-finding reports deserve particular weight as the work of independent investigators.

Both Sands and Reichler cited the submission in their closing arguments.

'Major repercussions for Israel case'

Becker, a professor of international law at Trinity College Dublin, said this was the first time a court would rule on mass human rights violations in a case brought by “a non-injured state acting to uphold international law”.

“Cases like The Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue,” Becker told MEE.

'Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel'

- Michael Becker, law professor

He said the judgment would be “a crucial opportunity for the ICJ to clarify and develop the law on genocide”, particularly on how intent can be established by inference.

“The core of Myanmar's argument is that actions that can reasonably be characterised as a counter-terrorism operation cannot simultaneously be treated as acts of genocide,” he said.

"Whether the ICJ accepts or rejects that view of genocidal intent will have major repercussions for South Africa's case against Israel at the ICJ," Becker explained, "where Israel has similarly claimed that an armed conflict with Hamas precludes a finding that Israel has simultaneously undertaken actions aimed at the physical destruction of the Palestinian population of Gaza.”

Becker said “recent claims that the ICJ may end up 'lowering the standard' to establish genocidal intent are misguided because they fail to acknowledge the ambiguities in the ICJ's pronouncements on genocidal intent”.

He added that the ruling would show how the court treats cases built largely on UN inquiry reports. Myanmar made attacks on the reliability of the fact-finding mission’s reports a central part of its defence, while the Gambia relied on the same reports extensively. 

“If the ICJ shows a reluctance to credit the findings of such reports, this will send a strong signal to South Africa, and potential litigants in other future cases, about the need to find other ways to support their claims,” he said.

A major UN inquiry last year already concluded that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza. Its chief investigator, Navi Pillay, told MEE at the time that her report used the same legal standard used by the ICJ in determining a finding of genocide and that it would "bear particular probative value and can be relied upon" by the court.

Israel submitted its response to South Africa's case in March. South Africa's reply is due in November 2027.

What the victims want

Mulvey said she is often asked what a ruling would mean for people in Cox's Bazar “who barely have $1 a day”.

“The short answer is yes, it makes a difference to the community,” she said. “It's important for them that the world's highest court recognises what happened to them.”

Many refugees told LAW researchers that compensation and punishment alone would not be enough. “What is the reason for the issue that happened to us? We need to fix the root cause,” one participant in the survey said. “If we want compensation, their punishment, and such things, I don't think we get our justice.

'For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable'

- Samir Sadaf, young Rohingya 

“Justice [meaning citizenship] is important for our children and grandchildren,” one woman who took part in the survey said. “If it prevails, they will have access to education and they will be able to become successful… in Myanmar.”

The Gambia's final submissions reflected some of these demands. It asked the court to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible and to provide reparations to the victims.

These include safe and dignified return, the restoration of property, the right to identify as Rohingya, and “full and equal citizenship”.

LAW has called for a trust fund for the Rohingya that would be linked to any reparations the court orders.

Samir Sadaf, a young Rohingya man who fled Rakhine as a child, described what justice would mean beyond a court ruling. 

“For me, justice means truth. It means that perpetrators must be held accountable,” he wrote in an article published by LAW. “Where there is justice, there should be safety, equal rights, freedom of movement, and dignity.”

Enforcing the law

ICJ judgments are binding and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of enforcing them. If a state refuses to comply, the matter can go to the UN Security Council, where China and Russia, both partners of Myanmar's military government, hold vetoes. 

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2017 operations, named himself president in April after contested elections.

“While it may prove impossible to enforce such a judgment while Myanmar continues to operate under military rule, compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community,” Becker said.

A ruling that Myanmar breached the convention “can also increase the pressure on third states to disengage from Myanmar until it demonstrates genuine reform”, he said.

Mulvey said LAW's victims' delegation will be in the courtroom when the judgment is read.

Salma, who sat in the court through the January hearings, said the Rohingya would not give up. “We won't go back without justice,” she said.
